Source: IRS Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025) https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sc
Also: 26 U.S.C. § 162, Trade or business expenses https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/162
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#fines-penalties

### Political contributions and lobbying: Usually not (Not deductible)
In plain English: Donations to candidates, campaigns and political parties, and most lobbying costs, can't be written off.
Keep as proof: Nothing to keep for a deduction
Common mistake: Running a campaign donation through the business as "marketing."
Rule: Contributions to candidates, campaigns and political parties aren't deductible, and neither are most costs of lobbying or trying to influence legislation or elections.
Limits: 0%. Part of your trade association dues may also be nondeductible if the group lobbies.
Records to keep: Nothing to keep for a deduction.
Applies to: All taxpayers.
Source: 26 U.S.C. § 162, Trade or business expenses https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/162
Also: IRS Publication 529 (Rev. 12/2020), Miscellaneous Deductions https://www.irs.gov/publications/p529
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#political-lobbying

### Club memberships: Usually not (Not deductible)
In plain English: Country clubs, golf clubs, gyms and other social or athletic clubs don't count, even if you meet clients there. Professional groups and the chamber of commerce are different.
Keep as proof: Nothing to keep for a deduction
Common mistake: Calling a country club or golf membership "networking." It still doesn't count.
Rule: Dues for clubs organized for business, pleasure, recreation or other social purposes, such as country clubs, golf and athletic clubs, airline and hotel clubs, aren't deductible.
Limits: 0%. Professional and trade associations, chambers of commerce and civic groups are different, and are generally deductible.
Records to keep: Nothing to keep for a deduction.
Applies to: All taxpayers.
Source: IRS Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses https://www.irs.gov/publications/p463
Also: 26 CFR § 1.274-2, Entertainment expenses (club dues) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.274-2
Also: 26 U.S.C. § 274, Disallowance of certain entertainment, etc., expenses https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/274
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#club-dues

### Gym and fitness memberships: Usually not (Not deductible)
In plain English: Gym, health club and fitness memberships are personal, even if staying fit helps you work. Meeting clients there doesn't change that.
Keep as proof: Nothing to keep for a deduction
Common mistake: Writing off a gym membership because staying fit helps you work, or because you sometimes meet clients there.
Rule: Gym, health club and fitness memberships are personal expenses. Dues to athletic clubs and other clubs organized for recreation or social purposes aren't deductible, even if you use them to meet clients.
Limits: 0%. Professional and trade associations, chambers of commerce and civic groups are different, and are generally deductible.
Records to keep: None needed for a deduction.
Applies to: All taxpayers.
Source: IRS Publication 463 (2025), Travel, Gift, and Car Expenses https://www.irs.gov/publications/p463
Also: IRS Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025) https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sc
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#gym

### Personal expenses: Usually not (Not deductible)
In plain English: Groceries, your gym, haircuts, vacations and family costs aren't business expenses, even if you pay with the business card. If something is used for both, only the business part counts.
Keep as proof: Keep business and personal spending in separate accounts
Common mistake: Paying personal bills from the business account and treating them as business expenses.
Rule: Personal, living and family expenses aren't business deductions, even if paid from a business account. When something is used for both, deduct only the business share.
Limits: 0% for the personal part. Paying a personal bill from the business account doesn't make it deductible.
Records to keep: Keep business and personal spending in separate accounts.
Applies to: All taxpayers.
Source: IRS Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025) https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sc
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#personal-expenses

### Charitable donations by your business: Usually not (Not deductible)
In plain English: Not as a business expense if you're a sole owner. On your personal return they can count if you itemize, and starting in 2026 up to $1,000 in cash gifts ($2,000 for married couples filing jointly) counts even if you don't.
Keep as proof: A written receipt from the charity; Proof you paid
Common mistake: Putting donations on your business schedule as a sole owner. They belong on your personal return.
Rule: A sole proprietor or single-member LLC can't deduct charitable contributions as a business expense on Schedule C. They may be deductible on your personal return under the charitable contribution rules.
Limits: Not on Schedule C. On your personal return, itemize on Schedule A, or, starting in 2026, deduct up to $1,000 of qualifying cash gifts ($2,000 married filing jointly) without itemizing. See Publication 526 and Publication 6196.
Records to keep: Written acknowledgments from the charity and proof of payment.
Applies to: Sole proprietors and single-member LLCs. Corporations follow their own charitable deduction rules.
Source: IRS Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025) https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sc
Also: IRS Publication 526 (2025), Charitable Contributions https://www.irs.gov/publications/p526
Also: IRS Publication 6196 (10-2026), Charitable Contribution Deduction Tips for Non-Itemizers https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p6196.pdf
Page: https://mfa-advisory.com/tools/is-it-deductible/#charitable-contributions

## Frequently asked questions

**Do you work with clients remotely?**
Yes — we serve clients nationwide through secure cloud tools, video meetings, and encrypted document exchange. Whether you're across the river or across the country, the service is the same.

**How is your pricing structured?**
You choose how you pay. Ongoing bookkeeping and advisory are usually a flat monthly fee, so your cost is predictable. One-off projects like cleanups and catch-up work get a project quote, and we also work on hourly contracts if you prefer to pay as you go. Bookkeeping pricing depends mainly on your monthly transaction volume, the number of accounts, complexity, and whether your books are on a cash or accrual basis. Everything is quoted up front after an initial consultation.

**What should I bring to the first call?**
For bookkeeping, tell us roughly how many accounts your business has, including bank accounts, credit cards and loans (an estimate is fine). That gives us your approximate monthly transaction volume, which, together with complexity, drives bookkeeping pricing. If you know whether your books are on a cash or accrual basis, mention that too; if not, we'll work it out together. For tax returns, have last year's return handy if you can.

**Can you clean up my QuickBooks or messy books?**
Absolutely. Our founder is a QuickBooks ProAdvisor, and cleanups and rebuilds are a specialty. We restructure your chart of accounts, correct misclassifications, reconcile every account, and hand back financials you can actually trust.

**I'm behind on my taxes. Can you help?**
Yes. Prior-year filings, catch-up bookkeeping, and estimated payment planning to get you current and keep you there. The sooner we start, the more options you have — reach out for a confidential conversation.

**What's actually included in fractional CFO work?**
Cash-flow forecasting, budgeting, KPI dashboards, pricing and margin analysis, financing support, and investor or board reporting — scaled to your business, at a fraction of a full-time hire.

**How do I switch from my current accountant?**
Painlessly. After a short consultation we handle the transition — requesting prior records, reviewing past filings, and setting up your systems — usually with no disruption to your operations.
